opus-5.5.text:
So I think there's a version of this question that people sometimes frame in very binary terms: either language models show that you can learn language from text alone, and therefore all the old poverty-of-the-stimulus arguments are wrong, or they're so different from people that they tell us nothing at all. I don't think either of those is quite right.

What these models give us, for the first time really, is an existence proof of a certain kind. We now have learners that don't have much in the way of hand-built linguistic structure, that are trained on nothing but strings, and that end up with surprisingly sophisticated grammatical behavior. They handle long-distance agreement, island constraints to some degree, filler-gap dependencies, things that people had argued were very hard to get from surface statistics. That doesn't settle how children do it, but it does change the shape of the argument. You can no longer say "this is in principle unlearnable from positive evidence" in quite the same way, because here's a system that learned something that looks a lot like it.

The big caveat, of course, is the data. These models see orders of magnitude more text than any child ever hears. So the interesting empirical questions become things like: how much of this competence survives when you scale the data down to something developmentally plausible? Which phenomena come out early and cheaply, and which ones seem to require enormous amounts of exposure? That's where I think the really informative experiments are. Efforts like the BabyLM challenge are pushing in exactly this direction, and what you find is that a lot of syntax comes in surprisingly fast, while other things lag behind.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that models are a tool we can actually intervene on, in a way we can't with kids. You can control exactly what's in the training data, remove every instance of a construction and see whether the model generalizes to it anyway, change the architecture's inductive biases, and then look inside at the representations it builds. That turns questions that used to be mostly philosophical into ones you can run controlled experiments on.

And finally there's the question of what "competence" even means here. Children aren't learning from text; they're learning in a grounded, interactive, social setting, with goals and communicative pressure. So I'd say language models tell us a lot about what's learnable from the distributional signal alone, which is a useful lower bound, and they give us a sharper sense of where the remaining puzzles really live: meaning, grounding, and efficiency of learning, rather than just the formal structure of syntax.

r001.rationale: The response describes sophisticated grammatical behavior and says models learned something that looks similar, but it does not clearly claim that text alone can support adult-like linguistic competence.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly says the models’ success “doesn't settle how children do it.”

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that there's a question that's been sitting in the background of linguistics and cognitive science for a long time, which is something like: how much of what we know about language could in principle be learned just from exposure to language, from the distribution of words and sentences, versus how much has to come from somewhere else, whether that's innate structure or grounding in the world or social interaction. And for most of the history of the field that's been an argument people had with thought experiments and with fairly small-scale computational models, because nobody could actually run the experiment.

What's changed is that we now have systems that are, in a pretty literal sense, the experiment. You take a model with relatively weak inductive biases, you expose it to an enormous amount of text and nothing else, and you can ask what it ends up knowing. And I think the honest answer is that it knows a lot more than many people expected. These models acquire a huge amount of syntactic structure, agreement, long-distance dependencies, pretty subtle things about what sentences are and aren't acceptable, and they do it without anyone building that structure in. So I think that's a real empirical result: you don't need a grammar hard-coded in advance to end up with something that behaves grammatically. That's informative about the learnability question, even if it doesn't settle it.

Now, the caveats matter a lot. The amount of data these models see is orders of magnitude more than a child sees, so they tell you something about what's learnable in the limit, not necessarily about what's learnable under human constraints. And the learner itself is very different. A transformer trained with gradient descent on next-word prediction is not a child, and I think we should be careful about treating the success of one as evidence about the mechanism in the other. What it does is set a kind of upper bound on how much signal is in the text alone, and that bound turns out to be surprisingly high.

The other thing I find interesting is where these models fall down, because that's often more diagnostic than where they succeed. They can be very good at form and much shakier on meaning, on reference, on what's actually true about the world, on knowing when a sentence describes something that could happen. And that's a nice natural experiment too, because it starts to carve out which parts of linguistic competence seem to come along for free with the distributional signal and which parts might really require grounding, or interaction, or some other source of information. So I don't think the lesson is "text is enough." I think the lesson is that we now have a tool for asking, piece by piece, what text is enough for, and that's a question we couldn't really ask before.

r001.rationale: The response says text alone can support substantial grammatical knowledge, but it does not claim that this amounts to adult-like linguistic competence; it emphasizes limits in meaning and grounding.

r002.rationale: It explicitly cautions that a transformer trained on text is not a child and that its success should not be treated as evidence about the human learning mechanism.

astra-6.text:
I think they give us a really interesting existence proof. One of the longstanding questions in language acquisition is how much of the structure of language you can learn just from the linguistic input, and how much has to come from some other source—whether that’s an innate bias or experience interacting with the world. These models show that you can get a surprisingly broad range of linguistic abilities from a fairly simple learning objective applied to text.

But we have to be careful about what the existence proof establishes. These systems typically see much more language than a child does, and they have different architectures and learning procedures. So showing that a model can acquire some ability from text doesn’t establish that children acquire that ability in the same way. Nor does it establish that the model has acquired everything we mean by linguistic competence.

Where I think this becomes especially useful scientifically is when we move beyond asking whether a model sounds fluent and start asking specific questions: What generalizations does it make? What kinds of input are necessary for those generalizations? How do those change as we vary the amount of data or the model’s learning biases? That gives us a way to test hypotheses about what information is available in language itself, even if we’re still some distance from an account of how children actually learn.

r001.rationale: The response says text can support a broad range of linguistic abilities, but does not claim that it can support adult-like linguistic competence; it explicitly cautions that the models may not acquire everything meant by linguistic competence.

r002.rationale: The response states that a model’s ability to acquire something from text does not establish that children acquire it in the same way.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they give us a kind of existence proof. There’s a long-standing question about how much of language you can learn from linguistic input alone, and how much requires other kinds of experience or some specifically linguistic innate structure. These models suggest that there’s a lot more information in the distribution of words than we might have thought. You can get remarkably sophisticated linguistic behavior from a fairly general learning procedure applied to text.

But we have to be careful about what that tells us about humans. These models often see vastly more text than a child does, and children are learning in a very different setting: they’re interacting with people, seeing things, and trying to accomplish things. So the existence of a successful text-trained model doesn’t establish that children learn language that way. What it does give us is a way to make these questions more concrete: which aspects of linguistic competence emerge from which kinds of data, with how much experience, and with what assumptions built into the learner? I think that’s where these models can be really useful as scientific tools.
